title: Dyatlov Pass: Why Did Nine Hikers Leave Their Tent?
description:
Their shoes were still inside. Why did nine hikers leave their tent on the slope?
Follow the case file, a later scientific model, and what remains unknown through checkable sources.

On February 26, 1959, searchers found an empty tent. Shoes and outerwear remained, and recorded footprints led downhill. What can the April examination of the tent fabric, the May closing report, a later snow slab model, and subsequent fieldwork each tell us? The model offers a possible reason for leaving the tent. It does not reconstruct everything that happened that night.

The visuals use cropped historical documents with sources and original evidence cards. The cards are not photos of the 1959 scene, measured snow profiles, or reconstructions of each person's actions. This video has Traditional Chinese narration and optional Traditional Chinese closed captions.

Main sources:
1959 closing report, pp. 384–387 (Russian transcript and scan index): https://dyatlovpass.com/case-files-384-387-ru
1959 tent examination, pp. 303–304 (Russian transcript and scan index): https://dyatlovpass.com/case-files-303-304-ru
Gaume and Puzrin, 2021 small snow slab model: https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-020-00081-8
Puzrin and Gaume, 2022 follow-up fieldwork: https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-022-00393-x

Sources checked: 2026-10-14.

h4v001.text: On February 26, 1959, searchers found a tent in the northern Ural Mountains.

h4v002.text: They cleared the snow and looked inside. None of the nine people were there.

h4v003.text: Most shoes and outerwear remained. Visible footprints led downhill.

h4v004.text: In April, examiners spread the tent fabric across a table.

h4v005.text: In May, a closing report finally set out to explain that night.

h4v006.text: Over 60 years later, two researchers revisited the question with a snow slab model.

h4v007.text: A year later, two local guides went onto a nearby snowy slope.

h4v008.text: Why did the nine leave a tent that still sheltered them from the wind?

h4v107.text: Searchers followed the remaining footprints downhill.

h4v009.text: The case file says ten set out; one turned back ill, and the others never returned.

h4v010.text: They were not all students; some were already working.

h4v011.text: Their last campsite was the slope tent the searchers had just found.

h4v012.text: What the searchers saw was the scene some time later.

h4v013.text: Remember the shoes inside? Investigators inferred a sudden departure.

h4v014.text: But that was an inference from objects. No one saw each person leave that night.

h4v105.text: From which side was that tear in the tent cut?

h4v015.text: Up close, the shoe and sock prints were not all alike.

h4v016.text: The closing report records some in thin socks, almost barefoot.

h4v017.text: There were also felt boot prints. The claim that everyone was barefoot does not hold.

h4v018.text: So how many sets of footprints can we actually distinguish?

h4v019.text: The report lists eight to nine sets of footprints.

h4v020.text: Another witness confirmed eight sets; a ninth was not confirmed.

h4v021.text: So the surviving prints cannot form nine complete routes.

h4v022.text: They point toward the valley and forest downhill.

h4v023.text: One examiner judged a stretch of tracks to look like ordinary walking.

h4v024.text: At least there, not everyone seemed to run all the way.

h4v025.text: But farther on, there were no equally complete prints to measure.

h4v026.text: Near the forest edge, snow covered the tracks. Searchers found a fire site there.

h4v108.text: Two people were found near the fire site.

h4v109.text: Three more lay on the straight line from the fire site to the tent.

h4v110.text: Their positions led the case file to suggest two were crawling toward the tent.

h4v030.text: Meanwhile, the tear in the tent still awaited another report.

h4v031.text: On April 16, examiners carefully inspected the remaining tent fabric.

h4v032.text: They examined the cuts and fine damage on the fabric's inner side.

h4v033.text: The answer from the fabric on the table: the cuts were made from inside.

h4v034.text: The direction was clear. But who cut it?

h4v035.text: The report names neither the person with the blade nor each person's exit.

h4v027.text: When the cut was identified, four people were still missing.

h4v028.text: In May, those four were found near a ravine.

h4v111.text: They were buried under more than four meters of snow.

h4v029.text: Their discovery also appeared in the later closing report.

h4v036.text: The report is four pages long; the stated cause comes at the end.

h4v037.text: On May 28, investigator Ivanov signed the decision to close the case.

h4v038.text: What cause did he ultimately give for that night?

h4v039.text: The May report mentioned earlier says: “a force of nature they could not overcome.”

h4v040.text: The original says natural, not supernatural.

h4v041.text: It does not name a specific mass of snow or when it slid.

h4v042.text: The case file stops there. An avalanche remained a possibility to explain.

h4v043.text: In 2019, prosecutors publicly announced a review.

h4v044.text: The next year's press conference put avalanches in the spotlight.

h4v045.text: It offered an explanation, but left a question: how did snow move on that slope?

h4v046.text: The slope does not look very steep on average.

h4v047.text: Even if snow could slide, why not right after the tent was pitched?

h4v048.text: In 2021, those two researchers modeled a small snow slab to explain the delay.

h4v049.text: A snow slab is a connected layer of snow that loses stability and moves as one.

h4v050.text: If a weaker layer lies beneath it, failure can start there.

h4v051.text: But from the surface, the terrain below may be invisible.

h4v052.text: The average slope and a short section above the tent are not the same thing.

h4v053.text: The model included a locally steeper step.

h4v054.text: That step lay beneath the snow; one distant photo cannot measure it.

h4v055.text: It assumed a weak layer followed local terrain, not a measured 1959 profile.

h4v056.text: Another condition was cutting a platform into the slope to pitch the tent.

h4v057.text: The cut changed the support for the snow above it.

h4v058.text: The weak layer and local terrain showed where failure might begin.

h4v060.text: But in this model, the slab need not slide as soon as the slope is cut.

h4v061.text: It also needs weight that builds gradually.

h4v062.text: The researchers assigned that weight to the wind.

h4v063.text: Wind lifts older snow from the ground and carries it elsewhere uphill.

h4v064.text: As snow accumulates above, the load on the slab gradually increases.

h4v065.text: The added weight presses on the weaker layer.

h4v066.text: How could the snow move? If the weak layer fails, the slab may slide.

h4v067.text: Why the delay? The opening model allows a slide hours later.

h4v068.text: The model can produce a plausible result, but not the accident's timing.

h4v069.text: The study also checked snow conditions against an estimated time interval.

h4v071.text: That night's snow depth, strength, and windblown snow were not fully measured.

h4v072.text: This is a small snow slab slide, not the whole mountain collapsing.

h4v073.text: Wind and time may change the marks on the snow surface.

h4v074.text: But we cannot say that is how the old traces definitely vanished.

h4v075.text: After the paper, the researchers decided to return to the mountains.

h4v076.text: In September 2021, a drone surveyed terrain near the possible campsite.

h4v078.text: That gave the model's terrain premise more support.

h4v079.text: But the drone measured ground, not the weak layer buried under snow in 1959.

h4v080.text: The team planned another winter trip to test the snow layers directly.

h4v106.text: Would the next slab traces match the model?

h4v081.text: The two local guides from the opening went onto nearby slopes in January 2022.

h4v082.text: They documented traces of two more recent snow slab avalanches.

h4v083.text: Those were on nearby slopes, not the same snow above the tent that night.

h4v084.text: The camera caught the aftermath, not the slab sliding.

h4v087.text: Not quite: the new slabs were softer, and the slopes steeper.

h4v088.text: There was no tent platform cut into the slope below them, either.

h4v091.text: Weather prevented the planned snow-layer and stability tests.

h4v092.text: After the news spread, the university and team both wrote about the trip.

h4v093.text: But both articles report the same observations.

h4v094.text: So how much does this model actually explain?

h4v099.text: The model also excludes movements after leaving the tent and body locations.

h4v100.text: What remains unknown does not give mysterious legends equal evidential weight.

h4v102.text: Back at the tent: a snow slide may have forced them out. No direct evidence.

h4v104.text: Subscribe to make sense of the clues.
